rv.q: "Paranormal Activity" knows what it wants to pull off and the execution is first-rate.
Barrett and Holloway come the closest I've ever seen — outside of a haunted house anyway — to achieving that same always-on-edge sensation onstage.

Wisely, for the thrilling 'Paranormal Activity' experience now on Broadway, the playwright Levi Holloway and the director Felix Barrett have jettisoned almost every characteristic of the movie franchise.
Paranormal Activity is a much more successful fright night.

The stage version of "Paranormal Activity" performs on an intimate and domestic scale yet delivers more thrills, chills and screams than Broadway has seen in years, and giving the franchise a legit afterlife.
That doesn't make the play a bad hang (I've had the time of my life on Star Tours), though its attempts to make itself more than just a vehicle for oohs and aahs grow tedious quickly.
The most impressive trick Paranormal Activity pulls off is making an entire theater — devotees and newcomers alike — afraid to look away, and giving them one hell of a good time while doing it.
Featuring cutting-edge stage effects and a story guaranteed to disrupt your sleep, it is the must-see Broadway show for scream queens.
Activity play is remarkable for the way it fits within a broader theatrical lineage, accentuated by its technical virtues.
This production will haunt you long after you leave the theater.
Paranormal Activity is by far the best entry for horror theatre we have seen on Broadway, perhaps ever?
What does matter is the mix of design elements aimed at scaring us.
Paranormal is the theatrical equivalent of a four-star-screamer, a summertime spooky movie.
This theatrical incarnation of Paranormal Activity faithfully, vividly, and unnervingly brings the movies’ gruesome sensibility to the stage.
It turns out to be a superbly staged ghost story that has audience members alternately screaming in terror and laughing in delight.
Fisher cooks up some chilling images that are wildly inventive and believable, even sitting very close to the stage.
Though playwright Levi Holloway's script falls far short of its aspirations of psychological complexity, it's as terrifying a play as has haunted Broadway in a long while.
Paranormal Activity can be marketed as a nightmare entertainment for the whole darned family.
The effects are more impressive than frightening, and “Harry Potter” and “Stranger Things” have already offered more elaborate stage magic.
This sometimes chilling, often funny theatrical attempt to create the equivalent of a horror film is ultimately more confusing than convincing.
Paranormal Activity is never boring, but its mechanical thrills aside, it is surprisingly anodyne.
For thrill seekers, fans of the film, or audiences curious about lesser-explored theatrical forms, Paranormal Activity is a must-see.
Paranormal Activity will have crept into your bloodstream like some unearthly virus, and you're unlikely to shake that sense of dread anytime soon.
Optimally staged, the production works on a micro- if not macro-level.
As a carnival ride, absolutely. As a play, no.
What Holloway has done with Paranormal Activity isn’t boring, but it doesn’t make for solid drama.

cn.t: Critics find "Paranormal Activity" a technically impressive scare machine with stellar sound design and effective jump scares, though most agree the thin script and psychological depth can't match the production's polished stagecraft.

vs.sum: The August Wilson Theatre offers good sightlines from most seats, although the rake isn't steep, which can cause issues if seated behind taller patrons. The theater has average comfort with decent legroom but tight seats. Its Italian-inspired design and cozy feel enhance the ambiance, making it a pleasant venue overall. Facilities are adequate, with standard amenities and helpful staff.

acc.note: Stair lift to orchestra; elevator between orchestra and mezzanine. Infrared headsets available.
